rationale:
Quota today is 1 long, 3 Shorts and 0 carousels. Everything sits inside the GLP-1 focus and uses four different pillars, with no pillar used more than twice.

**Long-form must be a search-demand format.** None of the last 7 long videos was one: Burping, Dehydration, Diarrhea, Injection Site, Fatigue, Birth Control and Stopping were all Lane A. I picked the approved-drug search long the playbook names as priority #5: "Orforglipron (Foundayo), what to expect, label only".
- "foundayo" is our top search term after EloraTZP, and the orforglipron long has earned 264 min, 111 of them from search.
- The 10-17 orforglipron video covered how the drug works and its Phase 3 trials. This one is a different angle: what starting it is like, built on the US label and Medication Guide, which are settled and fully checkable.
- The Nov 9 sleep apnea result appears only as a one-line hook in the intro, never in the body.

**Why not a long video on the NAION label change, even though it peaks at momentum 96.**
- It's still a moving news story, and we already ran eye Shorts on 11-09 and 11-10, including the FDA label change itself. A long video would repeat that angle within 30 days and carry fact-check risk.
- Blurry vision would be a third eye Short in 3 days, so I skipped it too.

**Shorts: 2 of 3 are felt symptoms or practical moments, all with the drug first in the title.**
- **S1 (08:00):** tirzepatide diarrhea, a calm "will it go away?" body-worry Short. It's a new Short angle that points to the 11-09 Diarrhea long video.
- **S2 (13:00):** the new randomized orforglipron sleep apnea result, framed as "what's confirmed". It's a spin-off of L1 and the only non-symptom Short.
- **S3 (20:00):** feeling full after a few bites, a Thanksgiving funnel Short that points to the existing Thanksgiving long video ahead of the Nov 18–27 peak.

**Topics left out.**
- Cagrisema-vs-tirzepatide waits for the full ObesityWeek presentation (Nov 14–17). It becomes an extra L2 within 48 h only if new randomized data is released then.
- Alcohol (marked caution, thin label evidence), lithium (case reports only) and hair (the Hair long video isn't verified clean yet) were deferred.

**Mix:** about half emerging or rising (sleep apnea, Thanksgiving) and half evergreen with a timely hook (Foundayo starters, diarrhea). S1 also carries a gentle myth correction: that diarrhea means something is wrong.

pieces.topic: Starting orforglipron (Foundayo), the once-daily GLP-1 pill approved in the US for chronic weight management: what to expect in the first weeks and months, based only on the US prescribing information and Medication Guide
pieces.angle: Orforglipron (Foundayo): what to expect when starting the once-daily pill, from the US prescribing information and Medication Guide only. First sentence: name orforglipron and give the short answer. Then a 'you' scenario. At 20–30 s, quote the label's exact wording that the tablet can be taken any time of day without food or water restrictions, with no comparison to other pills. Chapters: (1) the label's exact indication and population, plus 'not with other GLP-1 medicines'; (2) how to take it, label wording only, no doses or titration; (3) common GI side effects as label-table rates vs placebo, plus the label's timing wording; (4) untagged comfort tips, including fluids unless told to limit them; (5) ATTAIN-1 results as 72-week averages in adults without diabetes, then a one-line re-hook: a Phase 3 sleep apnea result was published in JAMA on Nov 9, it isn't an approved use, and a planned filing isn't approval; (6) warnings in label wording: boxed thyroid warning and MTC/MEN 2 contraindication, pancreatitis, gallbladder, dehydration and kidney, low blood sugar with insulin or sulfonylureas, plus one line on NAION quoted from the label if it's there, otherwise credited to the FDA's Nov 9 Drug Safety Communication; (7) questions for your prescriber, including 'tell them every medicine you take'. Scoped don't-stop line, 'Not personal advice' and the prescriber line, spoken and on screen. Title suggestion: 'Orforglipron (Foundayo): What to Expect on the Pill' (≤50 characters, fine). Thumbnail: pill bottle plus 'FIRST MONTH?'.
pieces.working_title: Orforglipron (Foundayo): What to Expect on the Pill
pieces.trend_stage: evergreen (approved-drug search demand, refreshed by the Nov 9 sleep apnea news)
pieces.why: Search-demand slot is due (0 of the last 7 longs were one). 'foundayo' is our top non-EloraTZP search term, and the content rests on the label, which keeps it fact-checkable. | fact-check: Topic is sound and fits the playbook's approved-drug search-long slot. Orforglipron (Foundayo) was FDA-approved on 1 Apr 2026 for chronic weight management in adults with obesity, or overweight plus at least one weight-related condition, alongside diet and activity. Sources: FDA approval letter https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/appletter/2026/220934Orig1s000ltr.pdf and Lilly Medical https://medical.lilly.com/us/products/answers/is-foundayo-orforglipron-approved-and-is-it-available-309937. The label has a boxed thyroid C-cell tumour warning and contraindications for MTC/MEN 2, and it says not to use it with other GLP-1 RAs. Four fixes are needed. (a) The angle calls the 20–30 s payoff 'the label's no food or water timing rule'. That's ambiguous and could be scripted backwards. Foundayo is taken once a day at any time, without food or water restrictions, unlike oral semaglutide (Rybelsus), which has a fasting rule. Quote the label's Dosage and Administration wording exactly and don't contrast it with Rybelsus numbers. (b) The FDA's Nov 9 Drug Safety Communication requires every GLP-1 RA label to add NAION to Warnings and Precautions. Sources: https://www.optometrytimes.com/view/fda-now-requiring-naion-warning-across-glp-1-receptor-agonist-class and https://www.healio.com/news/ophthalmology/20261109/fda-to-require-naion-risk-warning-for-glp1-therapies. The Foundayo label may not be updated yet. Viewers will have seen the news, so don't leave it out. If the label isn't updated, credit one calm line to the FDA communication, not the label. (c) Move the sleep apnea hook out of the opening 30 s. A topic that doesn't match the title is our worst retention pattern (Strength opened at 41%). Put it in chapter 5 or just before the ending as a re-hook, saying it isn't an approved use and that a planned filing isn't approval. (d) Per-arm adverse-reaction rates from the label table are fine, but they must not turn into a dose or titration schedule. Name the arms the way the table does and give no step-up timing. Also add the label's drug-interaction and other-medicines points as a plain 'tell your prescriber about every medicine you take' line. ATTAIN-1 results stay framed as 72-week averages in adults without diabetes.

pieces.topic: Tirzepatide diarrhea: is it normal, and when does it usually ease? Label rates per dose vs placebo, and the label's timing during dose increases
pieces.angle: Tirzepatide diarrhoea Short, tight arm. Sentence 1 (≤14 words) names tirzepatide and says diarrhoea is a common side effect in the trials. By 6 s: the Zepbound label rate per dose vs placebo over the trial period (one label only, named on the card), then 'in the trials it was more common during dose increases', in label wording, framed as a trial pattern, not a prediction. Tips (untagged): sip fluids unless you've been told to limit them; ask a pharmacist before any anti-diarrhoea product. When to get help: signs of dehydration (the label links it to kidney problems), or diarrhoea that's severe or won't settle. Emergency card: severe stomach pain that won't go away, with or without vomiting → stop and call your healthcare provider (label wording). Then: 'For anything that isn't one of those emergency signs, don't stop or change your medicine on your own.' Then 'Not personal advice' and the prescriber line, the Exp F line and the closing line. Title: 'Tirzepatide (Mounjaro) Diarrhea: Will It Ease? #shorts'. Post note: related-video target is the 11-09 Diarrhea long video.
pieces.working_title: Tirzepatide (Mounjaro) Diarrhea: Will It Go Away? #shorts
pieces.why: Felt symptom in the proven calm 'Is this normal?' format. No Short has covered diarrhea yet, and it funnels to the 11-09 Diarrhea long video. | fact-check: This is a proven body-worry format with a new fact (per-dose label rates), so the topic is approved. Two safety problems need fixing. (1) 'Severe stomach pain that won't go away' is the label's pancreatitis wording, and for pancreatitis the label says to stop and call your healthcare provider. So the don't-stop line must be scoped ('For anything that isn't one of those emergency signs…'), and the pancreatitis card must name its trigger and the stop-and-call instruction. (2) Use one label for the rates and say which one. The Zepbound (weight) and Mounjaro (T2D) tables differ, so don't mix them, and name placebo plus the timeframe. The dehydration red flag should use the label's wording that dehydration from vomiting and diarrhoea has been linked to kidney problems. The pharmacist line before any anti-diarrhoea product is fine and gets no source tag. Diarrhoea timing must stay the label's own wording ('during dose escalation'/'dose increases') as a trial pattern, with no promise about when it will stop. Add when to see a doctor: diarrhoea that's severe or won't settle, or signs of dehydration such as dizziness or very little urine. Title: avoid promising 'Will It Go Away?' as a yes. The script must answer with the hedge ('often eases, per the trials, but not for everyone').

pieces.topic: Orforglipron (Foundayo) and obstructive sleep apnea: the Phase 3 result presented at AHA 2026 and published in JAMA on Nov 9
pieces.angle: 13:00 'what's confirmed?' Short. Sentence 1 (≤14 words): 'Orforglipron, the Foundayo pill, cut sleep apnea severity in two trials, but it isn't approved for that yet.' AHI in one line: breathing pauses per hour of sleep. Population: adults with moderate-to-severe OSA and overweight or obesity, two randomized trials vs placebo over 52 weeks, one without PAP and one with PAP. Give the average AHI change per arm in events per hour, taken from the JAMA paper, naming the dose arm (and how AHI was measured in the PAP trial). Status: not approved for sleep apnea; Lilly plans to file with the FDA, and filing isn't approval. Tirzepatide (Zepbound) is approved in the US for moderate-to-severe OSA in adults with obesity, from separate trials, not head-to-head. 'If you use CPAP, don't stop or change it on your own.' Then 'Not personal advice', the prescriber line, the Exp F line and the closing line. Title: 'Orforglipron (Foundayo) and Sleep Apnea: What's Confirmed? #shorts'.
pieces.working_title: Orforglipron (Foundayo) Pill for Sleep Apnea: What's Confirmed? #shorts
pieces.why: Spin-off of L1. A fresh randomized result on a drug people search for by name, with low competition. | fact-check: The result is real. ATTAIN-OSA was two Phase 3 RCTs (n=363 in adults not on PAP, n=349 in adults on PAP), 52 weeks, in adults with moderate-to-severe OSA and overweight or obesity. It was presented at AHA on 9 Nov 2026 and published in JAMA (Malhotra et al., doi:10.1001/jama.2026.24080). Healio reports AHI falling by about 18–21 events/hour on orforglipron vs 4–5 on placebo without PAP, and about 17–18 vs 5 with PAP. Source: https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/20261109/oral-glp1-reduces-sleep-apnea-severity-improves-cardiometabolic-risk-factors. Lilly plans to file with the FDA by the end of 2026 (https://www.fiercepharma.com/pharma/lilly-heads-fda-phase-3-foundayo-win-sleep-apnea). Fixes: (1) The figures are ranges, which suggests more than one dose arm or estimand. The script must take one clearly named figure per arm from the JAMA paper (dose arm, estimand, and whether the PAP-group AHI was measured with PAP paused), not the press release's 'up to 44%'. Lead with events per hour vs placebo, with the percentage second if used at all. (2) Say 'two trials': one in people not using PAP, one in people using it. (3) Tirzepatide comparison: tirzepatide (Zepbound) is approved in the US for moderate-to-severe OSA in adults with obesity. That's obesity, not overweight, and tirzepatide is a GIP/GLP-1 medicine, so don't call it 'the GLP-1'. Separate trials, not head-to-head, no ranking. (4) The title 'Pill for Sleep Apnea' could read as approved. Use the 'What's Confirmed?' framing with the status by 6 s. (5) This counts as the week's single-trial Short.

pieces.topic: Why you may feel full or queasy after a few bites of a big holiday meal on tirzepatide (slower gastric emptying, label wording), and calm ways to pace the plate
pieces.angle: 20:00 funnel Short. Sentence 1: 'Full after three bites on tirzepatide? That's a known effect.' By 6 s: in label wording, tirzepatide delays gastric emptying (the label says this effect is largest after the first dose and gets smaller over time). Untagged tips: a small first plate with a protein you enjoy, then go back if you're still hungry; eat slowly; boxing leftovers is fine. No guilt, no 'bad' foods, no calorie talk. Caveat: if you also take insulin or a sulfonylurea, the label notes a higher risk of low blood sugar, so ask your prescriber how to handle meals. When to get help: vomiting that won't settle or signs of dehydration, so call your clinician; severe stomach pain that won't go away, with or without vomiting, means stop and call your healthcare provider. Then: 'For anything that isn't one of those signs, don't skip or change your injection around the holiday on your own.' Then 'Not personal advice', the prescriber line and the closing line (no Exp F line). Post note: related-video target is the Thanksgiving long video.
pieces.working_title: Tirzepatide (Mounjaro): Full After a Few Bites? #shorts
pieces.why: Seasonal spike building (momentum 93). Practical-moment format that funnels to the Thanksgiving long video ahead of the Nov 18–27 peak. | fact-check: A good funnel topic and a calm, non-diet framing. The Zepbound label's pharmacodynamics section says tirzepatide delays gastric emptying, and that the delay is largest after the first dose and gets smaller over time. Use that wording and don't overstate it as permanent. Without 'gastric emptying' and 'tirzepatide' in the title, it isn't a body-worry search, but 'Full After a Few Bites?' is fine. Additions: (1) a when-to-get-help line in label wording. Ongoing vomiting or signs of dehydration need a call to your clinician, and severe stomach pain that won't go away, with or without vomiting, means stop and call your healthcare provider. Then scope the don't-change line ('For anything that isn't one of those signs…'). (2) Keep the eating-disorder-safe framing: no 'eat less', no restriction praise, no 'bad' foods. 'Go back if you're still hungry' is good. (3) The low-blood-sugar caveat for insulin or sulfonylureas is right; keep it to the label's wording. (4) No holiday date words, per the angle. Holiday framing like 'a big holiday meal' is fine for a funnel Short, but don't say 'this Thanksgiving'.
